etymologies.etymologyHTML: From Middle French expectation, from Latin exspectātiō, from exspectō (“expect”). By surface analysis, expect +‎ -ation. Displaced native Old English wēn.

definitions.definition: The act or state of expecting or looking forward to an event as about to happen.

quote.citation: 1907 August, Robert W[illiam] Chambers, chapter IX, in The Younger Set, New York, N.Y.: D. Appleton & Company, →OCLC:
quote.text: “A tight little craft,” was Austin’s invariable comment on the matron; […]. ¶ Near her wandered her husband, orientally bland, invariably affable, and from time to time squinting sideways, as usual, in the ever-renewed expectation that he might catch a glimpse of his stiff, retroussé moustache.

definitions.definition: That which is expected or looked for.

quote.citation: 1922, Michael Arlen, “Ep./1/1”, in “Piracy”: A Romantic Chronicle of These Days:
quote.text: And so it had always pleased M. Stutz to expect great things from the dark young man whom he had first seen in his early twenties ; and his expectations had waxed rather than waned on hearing the faint bruit of the love of Ivor and Virginia—for Virginia, M. Stutz thought, would bring fineness to a point in a man like Ivor Marlay, […].

quote.citation: 1961 March, B.A. Haresnape, “Design on the railway”, in Trains Illustrated, page 145:
quote.text: Thus the B.R. diesel fleet today is composed of a rather assorted collection of designs. Some have proved to be remarkably satisfactory in service; others have so far not come up to expectations and I suppose it is doubtful whether any more orders for some types will be forthcoming.

definitions.definition: The prospect of the future; grounds upon which something excellent is expected to occur; prospect of anything good to come, especially of property or rank.

quote.citation: 1815 December (indicated as 1816), [Jane Austen], chapter 7, in Emma: […], volume (please specify |volume=I to III), London:  […]  [Charles Roworth and James Moyes] for John Murray, →OCLC:
quote.text: Emma was not sorry to be pressed. She read, and was surprized. The style of the letter was much above her expectation. There were not merely no grammatical errors, but as a composition it would not have disgraced a gentleman; the language, though plain, was strong and unaffected, and the sentiments it conveyed very much to the credit of the writer. It was short, but expressed good sense, warm attachment, liberality, propriety, even delicacy of feeling. She paused over it, while Harriet stood anxiously watching for her opinion, with a "Well, well," and was at last forced to add, "Is it a good letter? or is it too short?"

quote.citation: 1838 (date written), L[etitia] E[lizabeth] L[andon], chapter IX, in Lady Anne Granard; or, Keeping up Appearances. […], volume I, London: Henry Colburn, […], published 1842, →OCLC, page 108:
quote.text: Charles Penrhyn, for he was the object of Louisa's preference, had expectations—that term, so vague when those expectations depend upon others.

definitions.definition: The value of any chance (as the prospect of prize or property) which depends upon some contingent event.
(statistics) The first moment; the expected value; the long-run average value of a variable over many independent repetitions of an experiment.
(medicine, rare) The leaving of a disease principally to the efforts of nature to effect a cure.
